1:
What kind of authority the speaker claims is disputed at once. Keil and Delitzsch ground it in age and observation: wisdom and understanding increase with the years of those who earnestly seek them, and it is a father who here asks a willing ear for a wisdom of life gained through many years of experience. Adam Clarke says the same in a line, that the lessons following are taken from the speaker’s own experience. Matthew Henry claims much more, that he writes by divine inspiration and is a prophet, though he does not begin with the formula of the prophets; and Henry then defines the genre against two rivals, since these lectures are not designed to fill our heads with notions, with matters of nice speculation or doubtful disputation, but to guide us in the government of ourselves. He glosses the second half of the charge as speaking wisely, having knowledge ready at the tongue’s end for those with whom one converses, and adds that though it is the priest’s lips that are said to keep knowledge, those who are ready and mighty in the scriptures may be spiritual priests in their discourse as well as in their devotions. John Gill takes the wisdom offered to be a greater than the speaker’s own, and reads it of Christ.

The pairing of honey with wormwood brings in two kinds of parallel. Gill supplies both from Latin poets, one for the honeyed words and another for the saying that she has more aloes in her than honey. Charles Ellicott looks instead to scripture and finds the same reversal there, since the message that was in the mouth sweet as honey made the belly bitter, and its recipient met with much sorrow in making it known. Keil and Delitzsch supply the philology: the language treats bitterness and poison as related in meaning and in reality, and the word used means the curse in a cognate tongue; on the sword of the same verse they note that the older versions rendered it two-edged but that the Hebrew plural rather strengthens the sense poetically, as though the thing devoured with three or four edges. Clarke keeps the balance of the figure, that the bitterness is as excessive as honey is sweet, and adds a serpent to it, the poison infusing until the whole constitution of the victim is infected. Ellicott traces the smoothness of the mouth to a betrayal recorded elsewhere.

The sixth verse defeats them, and they divide on whose ignorance it describes. Keil and Delitzsch canvass the ways of joining the clause to what precedes and what follows, name several who have tried each, and reject outright the Jewish expositors who follow the Talmud in taking the verb as an address to the hearer, since a warning not to weigh the path of life yields no meaning suitable to the connection. Ellicott sets out both possibilities plainly: the English version makes the woman lead her victim by devious paths so that he shall not choose the path of life; but it may equally be rendered that, far from smoothing that path for herself, her own steps wander without her observing it. He prefers the second and draws a picture from it, of a woman who at last dares not think where her steps are leading and totters on as with her eyes shut until she falls to rise no more. Clarke and John Wesley both keep the first sense, that her arts are meant to prevent reflection, Wesley saying she transforms herself into several shapes and Clarke that it is impossible to conceive all her wiles, and that learning them in their varieties is part of the science first taught in that trade.
7:
Both of the voices that watch the structure notice a seam here, and describe it differently. Charles Ellicott takes it as a change of speaker, the teacher apparently ceasing to report his own father’s words and resuming in his own person. Keil and Delitzsch make it a discourse boundary instead: the new section springs out of the conclusion of the last and connects so closely that it looks like a continuation, yet its fresh opening and its confinement to social life secure its relative independence. They then make a negative observation easily missed, that neither here nor anywhere later in the discourse is there any reference to the criminal punishment inflicted on the adulterer, the whole warning being drawn from consequences. On the remedy prescribed, Ellicott is briefest and firmest: the great safeguard in such temptations, as all moralists with one mouth advise, is flight. John Gill puts the same as avoidance of a contagion, shunning her as one would the pest or a loathsome carcass and going a good way about rather than come within sight. Adam Clarke gives a reason for the door in particular, that about it are exhibitions with a natural tendency to excite impure thoughts.

What is forfeited is read as vigour by most and as property by one. Ellicott renders the word freshness or vigour and the years as the best years of a life; Keil and Delitzsch make it the bloom of youth and the years of youthful fulness of strength; John Wesley combines dignity, reputation and the strength of body and mind. Gill leans toward wealth and reputation while allowing bodily vigour, and cites two versions rendering it strength of body. On the cruel one to whom these years are given, Ellicott names the temptress or her associates, whose sole idea is plunder, and Keil and Delitzsch report that the ancients referred the word to death and the devil. Clarke fills the word out from the world he knew: though all the blandishments of love dwell on the tongue, cruelty has its throne in the heart, and such persons will rob and murder those who give them their strength and their years; murders have often taken place in brothels as well as robberies, for that vice is one of the parents of cruelty.

The groaning at the end draws a striking convergence. Gill hears a roar as of a lion, Clarke says the word is often applied to the growling of a lion and the hoarse incessant murmuring of the sea, and Keil and Delitzsch add that it is used elsewhere of the roaring sea and the growling lion and here of the hollow groaning of men, being a word that echoes the natural sound. They also note that the Greek read a different word here and rendered it thou shalt repent, and call this a happy exchange, since the two verbs in a cognate tongue mean respectively to breathe hard and to repent. Clarke leaves the philology for testimony: in the line of his duty he has often been called to the death-bed of such persons, where groans and shrieks were incessant through the pains in their bones and flesh, and whoever has witnessed such a scene will perceive with what propriety this is written. On the last verse Ellicott offers two senses, that the speaker had almost fallen into every sin and might have committed any openly, or that he might have suffered the extremest punishment at the hands of the congregation. Keil and Delitzsch canvass the same alternatives, report one scholar taking the word directly of stoning and another of the totality of evil, and conclude for every kind of evil while allowing the other may be thought of alongside.
15:
Marriage is prescribed here as a remedy, and Matthew Henry defends the prescription against the charge of meanness. Let none complain that God has dealt unkindly in forbidding pleasures they naturally desire, since he has provided for their regular gratification: a man may not eat of every tree of the garden, but he may choose one and freely eat of that, for nature will be content with one and lust with nothing. Henry twice quotes a poet in support, once for the maxim that if God had laid all common man would certainly have been the encloser, and once for the rule that a man should wholly abstain or else wed; and he adds that the allowed pleasures of marriage, however wicked wits may ridicule them, far transcend the forbidden ones. John Gill reaches for an older parallel, reporting a claim that a Greek philosopher took from the Hebrews a law forbidding husbandmen to draw water from others for their lands until they had dug in their own ground. Adam Clarke makes the counsel run both ways, since the wife is to see that she reverence her husband and not tempt him by inattention or unkindness to seek elsewhere what he cannot find at home.

What the streams dispersed abroad are is read three ways. Gill, Clarke and John Wesley all take them for children lawfully begotten, Gill adding that they are dispersed when grown children marry into other families and become fountains to others. Keil and Delitzsch keep the figure at the physical level and press its terms in two learned languages. Charles Ellicott leaves generation aside altogether and reads the next verse of privacy, that the deepest joys and sorrows of each heart are sacred and cannot be shared, and that the relations of family life are the same, strangers having no part in them. On the same verse the others think of paternity: Gill says a man who keeps to a virtuous wife is satisfied the children are his own, Clarke that a brood born outside marriage is no credit to any man however numerous, and Keil and Delitzsch that such a child belongs to no one in particular, its father being obliged for his honour to deny it before the world. Clarke, having offered his own rendering of the fountain, breaks off deliberately: the allusion is delicate and correct, he says, but anatomical allusions must not be pressed into detail in a commentary on scripture — the very detail that the note standing beside his supplies at length.

The two animals are identified with some care. Keil and Delitzsch deny that the second is the gazelle, which has another name given for its elegance, and make it the chamois; they derive the first perhaps from the weapon-power of its horns, and observe that both are common in the poetry of that region as figures of female beauty for the delicacy of their limbs and their lively black eyes. Ellicott says the same of their grace and speed and lustrous eyes and adds that both are remarkable for affection to their young; Gill offers instead that princes kept such creatures tame, washing and combing and adorning them. On the degree of indulgence commended, two enter a caution: Wesley says the word is hyperbolical and that excess in the marriage bed is plainly possible, and Keil and Delitzsch that government, moderation and restraint remain a duty within marriage as well. Keil and Delitzsch also record, and decline, the allegorical reading of this whole section taken by the ancients and by one modern; Gill supplies exactly that reading, making the streams the truths of the Gospel and the loving hind the pure church against the apostate one.
21:
The closing argument turns on being watched, and it is put three ways. Charles Ellicott states it plainly, that another reason for avoiding sin is the certainty of detection by the Judge whose eyes run to and fro through the whole earth. John Gill argues from the lesser case to the greater: the adulterer seeks the twilight and flatters himself with secrecy, and it is precisely because men would be ashamed if their actions were known to other men that they take such pains to hide them; if the fear of human knowledge deters so much, the consideration of the divine omniscience should weigh far more. Keil and Delitzsch state what the verse is doing in the argument, that irregular intercourse is here proved to be the commencement of a fool’s ruin, and pause over whether the phrase is an adverbial accusative, straight before the eyes, or the nominative of the predicate, the ways of a man being themselves the object on which those eyes are fixed.

On the cords of the following verse two of them arrive independently at the same psychology. Adam Clarke sets it out as a sequence: most who follow unlawful pleasures think they can give them up whenever they please, but sin repeated becomes customary, custom soon engenders habit, and habit in the end assumes the form of necessity, so that the man is bound with cords of his own making. Gill describes the same illusion from the other end, that the adulterer fancies his lusts will weaken as he grows old and that repentance will then be available, but finds himself mistaken, growing more hardened and confirmed and left with neither the will nor the power to repent. Gill adds a second sense, that the words may equally be taken of guilt and punishment, since the horrors of a guilty conscience need no other officer to make the arrest.

The last verse is read three ways by Gill alone. It may mean that those who hated and rejected instruction in health should justly have none given them when they come to die; or, better, that the man dies because of instruction, that is, because he would not bear it, which he supports from two Jewish commentators; or that the word means correction and amendment rather than teaching. Keil and Delitzsch render the second clause as staggering to ruin in the fulness of folly, and John Wesley glosses the whole as dying in one’s sins and going astray from the way of life. Clarke accepts the sentence and then declines to make it absolute: this is most likely, he says, and it is a general case, but even these may repent and live.
